newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SPANISH ARMADA OF SANCHEZ VICARIO AND MARTINEZ WIN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SPANISH ARMADA OF SANCHEZ VICARIO AND MARTINEZ WIN.

text.p: The Spanish Fed Cup armada of Arantxa Sanchez Vicario and Conchita Martinez secured berths in the quarter-finals of the season-ending Chase Championships on Wednesday.

The third-seeded Sanchez Vicario withstood the fireball-serving Brenda Schultz-McCarthy for a 6-4 7-6 win and the fourth-seeded Martinez overcame a sore left hamstring to survive a three-set scare against the lowest-ranked player in the field, Judith Wiesner, in opening-round matches.

Although she was treated by the trainer after the second set, Martinez moved easily and comfortably around the court in the final set to complete the 6-1 3-6 6-4 win in the $2 million tournament at Madison Squre Garden.
Sanchez Vicario's victory despite 16 aces from the unseeded 6 foot, 2 inch (1.88 metres) Dutchwoman was her first in the tournament since reaching the final in 1994.

"I came more prepared this year. I came really fresh. That was my goal, to stay a bit longer," said Sanchez Vicario, who has teamed with Martinez to lead Spain to the Fed Cup final the last six years, winning in 1991 and 1993 through 1995.
Fifth-seeded Czech Jana Novotna completed the quarter-final lineup by beating South African Amanda Coetzer 6-4 6-1 in the final match on the programme before 8,567 fans.

Schultz-McCarthy had at least one ace in eight games and one in the tiebreaker, but Sanchez Vicario still managed to get the only service break in the first set and won three points off her serve to win the tiebreaker 7-4.

"They have always said I have a very good return and today it showed," said Sanchez Vicario, a two-time French Open winner as well as the 1994 U.S. Open champion. "We all know that she has the biggest serve and fastest serve in women's tennis. I just had to be patient and be tough mentally."
Martinez, whose only Grand Slam singles title came at Wimbledon in 1994, felt her leg stiffen late in the second set against the Austrian, ranked 19th in the world.
"I hurt it about three days ago and suddenly it felt worse," Martinez said of the injury. "It's not a huge injury, but I was feeling tighter and tighter during the match."
Martinez felt a little better after taking a 4-1 lead in the last set before Wiesner rallied to take the next three games.
But the Spaniard wrapped up the one hour and 59 minute struggle in the next two games, losing just three points.
The hard-fought win put Martinez into the quarter-finals of the season-ending tournament for the fifth year in a row.

Martinez, 24, will not have much time to rest. She is scheduled back on the court Thursday against Iva Majoli, the Croatian teenager who upset last year's runner-up, Anke Huber of Germany, on opening night.
"We'll keep our fingers crossed and the trainers are working on it and we'll see what happens," Martinez said.

Wiesner, at 30 the oldest player in the elite 16-player field, was making only her second appearance in the event. She suffered a first-round loss in 1990 and seemed destined to make another quick exit after losing the first set in 30 minutes.
Wiesner started her comeback by breaking Martinez for a 3-1 second set lead.
"I was playing more aggressive and serving better," Wiesner said of the second set, when she had 15 winners and lost just six points on her first serve.
Martinez and Wiesner were playing for the first time in three years, but little had changed with the passage of time as the Spaniard won for the seventh time in a row.
"We both play from the baseline and she is just more consistent," Wiesner said. "And with the topspin she's playing, she keeps me off-balance a lot, so I have a problem reading that."
